status: COMPLETE — all of §0–§11 + Defaults table + Source ledger captured in sdd-1..sdd-45 (research read in full; no context dropped). sections_accounted maps every section to its rules.
note: Repo-agnostic practitioner guide for turning a plain-English requirement into a human-reviewable, then executable, specification: the discovery→formulation→automation pipeline, Gherkin as one labelled-example syntax for the formulated stage, acceptance criteria as the definition of done, specification-by-example/living documentation, keeping spec/code/tests synchronized, and the anti-patterns that let a spec rot. Cucumber/Gherkin and Dan North's original BDD article are the primary verified sources; Gojko Adzic's Specification by Example is cited only via Manning's official book page because the book's own chapter text could not be independently fetched (sample-chapter PDF is scanned images with no extractable text; specificationbyexample.com no longer resolves) — that dead-end is disclosed in sdd-33 rather than papered over. Genesis agents apply this whenever they write or review a plain-English spec, a Gherkin/BDD feature, or acceptance criteria for any change.

rules.text: A spec-driven example is three things at once: a specification, a piece of documentation, and a test. Once formulated and automated, examples are 'an executable specification of the system' — there is no separate 'real spec' hiding elsewhere that tests merely check against; the example IS the spec. [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference — 'Example'.]

The pipeline has three practices, run in order: Discovery (what the system COULD do) → Formulation (what it SHOULD do, written so both humans and computers can read it) → Automation (what it ACTUALLY does, checked by running code). Skipping discovery to jump straight to writing Gherkin is the most common failure mode — 'you won't get much joy from the other two practices until you've mastered discovery.' [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/bdd/ — 'Three practices'.]

A story's behaviour IS its acceptance criteria — not a checklist alongside it. 'If the system fulfils all the acceptance criteria, it's behaving correctly; if it doesn't, it isn't.' Dan North's contribution was making that criteria EXECUTABLE, so 'done' is a command's exit code, not an opinion. [VERIFIED, dannorth.net/blog/introducing-bdd/.]

The hardest problem in building software is deciding precisely what to build — Cucumber's docs open their case for BDD with Fred Brooks: 'The hardest single part of building a software system is deciding precisely what to build.' SDD's primary output is therefore not tests or docs but the right conversations at the right time; documentation and automated tests are 'nice side-effects' of shared understanding, not the goal itself. [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/bdd/ — 'Discovery: What it could do', quoting Fred Brooks.]

BDD closes the business/technical gap through three named mechanisms: (1) collaboration across roles for shared understanding, (2) rapid small iterations for feedback, (3) system documentation automatically checked against the system's actual behaviour — done 'by focusing collaborative work around concrete, real-world examples that illustrate how we want the system to behave.' [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/bdd/ — 'What is BDD?'.]

predicate.spec: the team's BDD/SDD practice visibly exercises all three mechanisms — cross-role collaboration sessions, small-iteration delivery, and specs wired to automated checks against real behaviour — not just one of the three.

rules.text: SDD/BDD is not a rival to agile — it assumes one. It 'does not replace your existing agile process, it enhances it'; think of it as 'a set of plugins' for a team already planning in small increments. [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/bdd/ — 'BDD and agile'.]

Run the three practices in order, never skipped: Discovery (structured conversations/workshops around real-world examples, surfacing gaps and deferrable scope) → Formulation (write the found example as structured documentation readable by humans AND computers) → Automation (wire it to executable checks against real system behaviour). [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/bdd/ — 'Three practices'.]

predicate.spec: a spec-driven change shows a discovery conversation (workshop notes, example-mapping cards, or equivalent) before a formulated scenario exists for it, and the formulated scenario exists before automation is written against it.

rules.text: Formulating examples collaboratively, in a medium readable by both humans and computers, does double duty: the whole team gives feedback on the shared vision, and by writing it together the team establishes 'a shared language for talking about the system' that reaches 'all the way down into the code.' A specification formulated solely by one role after the fact forfeits this second effect. [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/bdd/ — 'Formulation: What it should do'.]

predicate.spec: formulated scenarios are produced through a cross-role collaborative session (not authored solely by one role after implementation) and use shared, agreed-on domain terminology.

rules.text: A Gherkin document's primary keywords are Feature, Rule (Gherkin 6+), Example/Scenario, the step keywords Given/When/Then/And/But (or *), Background, and Scenario Outline/Scenario Template with its Examples/Scenarios table; secondary keywords are Doc Strings ('"""'), Data Tables ('|'), Tags ('@'), and Comments ('#'). Every non-blank line starts with one of these except permitted free-form description lines. [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference — 'Keywords'.]

predicate.spec: the formulated spec file uses only these primary/secondary keywords to structure content; free text appears only where the reference permits it (under Example/Background/Scenario Outline/Rule).

rules.text: Feature gives a high-level description and groups related scenarios; free-form text beneath it is ignored by the runner but preserved for reporting, and a single file holds exactly one Feature. A Feature accumulating 'lots and lots' of scenarios is a signal it is actually describing more than one feature. [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference — 'Feature'; cucumber.io/docs/bdd/who-does-what/ — 'Scenarios'.]

predicate.spec: each spec file contains exactly one Feature: declaration, and a feature whose scenario count has grown very large has been reviewed for a split.

rules.text: Rule (added in Gherkin 6) represents one business rule and groups the scenarios that illustrate it, making 'this set of examples illustrates the SAME rule' explicit in the document structure instead of implicit. [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference — 'Rule'.]

predicate.spec: where two or more scenarios in a feature illustrate the same underlying business rule, they are grouped under a shared Rule block rather than left as unrelated top-level scenarios.

rules.text: Each Example/Scenario is a concrete example illustrating a business rule, built from Given(context)/When(event)/Then(outcome) steps; recommended 3-5 steps, because too many erodes 'its expressive power as a specification and documentation.' 'In addition to being a specification and documentation, an example is also a test. As a whole, your examples are an executable specification of the system.' [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference — 'Example'.]

predicate.spec: each scenario has roughly 3-5 steps and follows Given(context)→When(event)→Then(outcome) ordering; scenarios well outside that step count are reviewed for a split.

rules.text: Background hoists Given steps repeated across EVERY scenario in a Feature (repetition signals they're incidental, not essential); runs before each scenario after any Before hooks. Keep it short (~4 lines), vivid (memorable names, not 'User A'), and never use it to bury complicated state the reader needs to see. [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference — 'Background' and 'Tips for using Background'.]

predicate.spec: Background contains only Given steps common to every scenario in the feature, stays within roughly 4 lines, and does not hide state a reader needs in order to evaluate the scenario's correctness.

rules.text: Scenario Outline (alias Scenario Template) collapses near-duplicate scenarios into one template with <param>-delimited placeholders, run once per data row in its Examples/Scenarios table (header row not run); placeholders may also appear in the outline's description and in multiline step arguments. [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference — 'Scenario Outline' and 'Examples'.]

predicate.spec: scenarios differing only in data values are expressed as one Scenario Outline with an Examples table, not copy-pasted per value combination.

rules.text: Doc Strings (delimited by triple double-quotes or triple backticks) pass a larger text block as a step's last argument, dedented relative to the opening delimiter; Data Tables (|-delimited) pass structured tabular data, escaping a literal | as \|, a newline as \n, and a backslash as \\ inside a cell. [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference — 'Doc Strings', 'Data Tables', 'Table Cell Escaping'.]

predicate.spec: multi-line text passed to a step uses a Doc String, and structured/tabular step data uses a Data Table with correctly escaped pipe/newline/backslash characters inside cells.

rules.text: A Gherkin file's spoken language must match the language users and domain experts actually use — 'translating between two languages should be avoided.' Gherkin ships localized keywords for 70+ languages, selected per-file via a leading '# language: <code>' comment (default English). [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference — 'Spoken Languages'.]

predicate.spec: a spec's keyword language matches the language domain experts use, declared via a '# language:' header when it is not the tool's default.

rules.text: @Tags group Features/Scenarios (e.g. for selective execution) independently of file/directory layout, placed above the tagged element. Comments (#) are free text ignored by the parser, with one reserved exception: a '# language:' header as the first line of a file sets that file's spoken language. [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference — 'Feature' (tags note) and 'Spoken Languages'.]

predicate.spec: cross-cutting grouping (e.g. 'run only smoke scenarios') is expressed via tags, not via directory-naming conventions the runner has no notion of.

rules.text: Given steps describe the initial context — 'the scene of the scenario,' typically past-tense — and put the system in a well-defined state. Avoid describing user interaction in a Given; if writing use cases, Givens are the preconditions. Multiple givens chain with And/But. [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference — 'Given'.]

predicate.spec: Given steps set up state only (no simulated user action) and read as something already true before the scenario's event occurs.

rules.text: When steps describe one event or action. Apply the 'imagine it's 1922' test: could a person do this without a computer? A step reading like a UI mechanic instead of a domain action has smuggled implementation/technology assumptions into the spec — those belong in the step definition, never the Gherkin text. [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference — 'When'.]

predicate.spec: each When step names exactly one domain-level action free of UI/technology detail (e.g. 'Withdraw money,' not 'click the withdraw button and enter 20 in the amount field').

rules.text: Then steps assert an expected, OBSERVABLE outcome — 'something that comes out of the system (report, user interface, message), and not a behaviour deeply buried inside the system (like a record in a database).' 'While it might be tempting to implement Then steps to look in the database — resist that temptation!' [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference — 'Then'.]

predicate.spec: Then steps assert on a user/external-system-observable output, never directly on internal storage state.

rules.text: And/But are readability sugar for consecutive same-kind steps — Cucumber's matcher ignores the leading keyword entirely, so a Given and a Then with identical text ARE the same step (a duplicate). This forces 'a less ambiguous, more clear domain language': e.g. 'Given/Then there is money in my account' collide, while 'my account has a balance of £430' phrasing does not. [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference — 'Steps' and 'And, But'.]

predicate.spec: no two steps of different intent share identical wording once the leading Given/When/Then/And/But keyword is stripped; a collision is resolved by more precise domain language, not by a workaround in the automation layer.

rules.text: Treat 'can this be phrased as a Given(context)/When(event)/Then(observable-outcome) triple' as the operational test for whether prose is actually a specification yet. Prose with no discernible prior context, no single event, or a Then not phrasable as an observable assertion is untestable by construction — it needs another discovery/formulation pass, not a more strongly-worded comment.
rules.reviewer_criterion: For any requirement claimed as 'specified,' can a reviewer point to its Given (context), When (event), and Then (observable assertion) — and if not, has it correctly been treated as not yet spec-ready rather than shipped as prose?

rules.text: 'A story's behaviour is simply its acceptance criteria: if the system fulfils all the acceptance criteria, it's behaving correctly; if it doesn't, it isn't.' Acceptance criteria are therefore not a checklist run against the definition of done — they ARE the definition of done. [VERIFIED, dannorth.net/blog/introducing-bdd/ — "BDD provides a 'ubiquitous language' for analysis".]

predicate.spec: a story/change is declared done only when every one of its stated acceptance-criteria scenarios passes, not on a separate, informally-judged basis.

rules.text: The story template 'As a [X], I want [Y], so that [Z]' forces the value to be named at definition time: 'its strength is that it forces you to identify the value of delivering a story when you first define it.' A story degrading to '...so that [I just do, ok?]' is a legible signal to descope it. [VERIFIED, dannorth.net/blog/introducing-bdd/ — "BDD provides a 'ubiquitous language' for analysis".]

predicate.spec: every accepted story states an X/Y/Z (role/feature/benefit) triple, and a story whose 'so that' is vacuous or unnamed is flagged for descoping rather than accepted as-is.

rules.text: Dan North's acceptance-criteria scenario template — 'Given some initial context (the givens), When an event occurs, Then ensure some outcomes' — was built 'loose enough that it wouldn't feel artificial or constraining to analysts but structured enough that we could break the story into its constituent fragments and automate them.' This is the documented origin of Gherkin's Given/When/Then. [VERIFIED, dannorth.net/blog/introducing-bdd/ — "BDD provides a 'ubiquitous language' for analysis".]

predicate.spec: acceptance-criteria scenarios follow the Given(context)/When(event)/Then(outcome) template rather than free-form prose.

rules.text: 'Acceptance criteria should be executable': the given/event/outcome fragments are fine-grained enough to be represented directly in code. North's original JBehave mapped each Given to its own class, one class for the Event, and classes for the Outcomes, wired against a shared 'world,' making fragments reusable across scenarios/stories, not just readable. [VERIFIED, dannorth.net/blog/introducing-bdd/ — 'Acceptance criteria should be executable'.]

predicate.spec: automated acceptance criteria are composed of reusable, independently-testable context/event/outcome fragments, not one monolithic script per scenario.

rules.text: 'Who should be writing Gherkin documents... depends on several factors, such as team structure, skills, culture, process and more' — no single universal answer. Durable default: whole team collaborates early while style is being established; later a developer+tester pair writes it efficiently, as long as output is actively reviewed by the product owner/business representative. [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/bdd/who-does-what/ — 'Writing Gherkin'.]

predicate.spec: no scenario is formulated by a single role in isolation without product-owner/business-rep review before it is treated as agreed.

rules.text: The 'Three Amigos' meeting turns a user story into clean Gherkin scenarios via at least three voices: the product owner (scope), the tester, and the developer (implementation detail); 'it is essential that all of these roles have conversations to discover examples together.' Not a one-time, exactly-three-person, kickoff-only ritual — hold it repeatedly. [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/bdd/who-does-what/ — 'The Three Amigos'.]

predicate.spec: a nontrivial new scenario set has evidence of at least a product/business, a quality/testing, and a development perspective having been consulted, not authored by one role alone.

rules.text: BDD's ubiquitous-language move — North and Chris Matts defining a ubiquitous language for 'the analysis process itself,' borrowing the term from Eric Evans's Domain-Driven Design (business vocabulary 'permeates right into the codebase') — means the same words a domain expert uses in conversation should appear in the Given/When/Then text AND in the code. [VERIFIED, dannorth.net/blog/introducing-bdd/ — "BDD provides a 'ubiquitous language' for analysis".]
rules.reviewer_criterion: Can a domain expert with no engineering background read the scenario's nouns and verbs and recognize their own vocabulary — or does it lean on internal/technical terms the business side doesn't use?

rules.text: A discovery workshop is a structured conversation, held BEFORE formulation, centered on real-world examples from the user's perspective; it grows shared understanding of needs/rules/scope and may reveal gaps. 'The scrutiny of a discovery session often reveals low-priority functionality that can be deferred from the scope of a user story.' [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/bdd/ — 'Discovery: What it could do'.]

predicate.spec: a discovery workshop (or equivalent structured conversation around real-world examples) precedes formulation for nontrivial new scope, and scope-deferral decisions from it are recorded.

rules.text: Example Mapping runs discovery on four card colours: yellow = the story on top, blue = each rule/acceptance-criterion beneath it, green = examples illustrating a rule, red = an unanswered question/assumption captured so the group can keep moving. Continue 'until the group is satisfied that the scope of the story is clear, or we run out of time.' [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/bdd/example-mapping/ — 'How it works'.]

predicate.spec: a formulated scenario traces back to a blue rule card that traces back to a yellow story card from an actual mapping/discovery session, and open questions are captured as red cards rather than silently resolved or ignored.

rules.text: Gojko Adzic's Specification by Example distills team case studies into seven collaborative patterns ('Seven patterns, fully explored in this book, are key to making the method effective'). Four main benefits per the publisher: 'it produces living, reliable documentation; it defines expectations clearly and makes validation efficient; it reduces rework; and, above all, it assures delivery teams and business stakeholders that the software that's built is right for its purpose.' [VERIFIED, manning.com/books/specification-by-example.]

predicate.spec: a team applying specification-by-example can name which of the four stated benefits (living documentation, clear/efficient validation, reduced rework, right-software assurance) a given practice change is intended to produce.

rules.text: Disclosed limitation: this guide could NOT independently verify the seven patterns' individual names/mechanics against the book's own text — the Manning sample-chapter PDF is a scanned-image PDF with no extractable text (confirmed by attempted extraction: only embedded-image/XMP-metadata binary streams returned), and specificationbyexample.com no longer resolves (DNS failure). Independent secondary summaries converge on: deriving scope from goals, specifying collaboratively, illustrating using examples, refining the specification, automating validation without changing specifications, validating frequently, evolving a documentation system — but this list is [INFERRED] from secondary aggregation, not a verbatim primary quote; verify against the book directly before treating one pattern's detailed mechanics as settled fact.

'Living documentation' is the convergence point of specification-by-example and BDD's own stated goal: documentation 'automatically checked against the system's behaviour.' Unlike a wiki page, a living-documentation scenario cannot silently drift out of date — if the system stops matching it, the scenario fails (red) rather than quietly becoming wrong. [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/bdd/ — 'What is BDD?'; corroborated by manning.com/books/specification-by-example's 'living, reliable documentation' framing.]

predicate.spec: formulated specs are wired to automation such that a behaviour change with no matching spec update produces a failing (red) run, not merely an unreviewed diff.

rules.text: Because automation ties the formulated spec directly to live system behaviour, an out-of-date scenario doesn't rot silently like a wiki page — it goes red. The same executable-specification property that makes an example a test (sdd-1, sdd-12) is what makes drift detectable at all. [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/bdd/ — 'documentation automatically checked against the system's behaviour', applied to the drift question.]

predicate.spec: CI (or an equivalent gate) runs the formulated specs on every change, so a spec/behaviour mismatch is caught as a failing run rather than discovered later by inspection.

rules.text: When behaviour intentionally changes, update the scenario as part of the SAME change, not the code first with the scenario patched up afterward. Because the scenario is plain-English and business-readable, a deliberate behaviour change surfaces in review as a visible, readable scenario edit; a scenario edited only to make a stale test pass with no explanation of why behaviour changed is a smell.
rules.reviewer_criterion: For a change that alters observable behaviour, does the reviewable diff include the scenario edit alongside the code edit, in a form a non-engineer reviewer could read and understand what changed and why?

rules.text: Collaborative formulation (sdd-8, sdd-27) is itself a synchronization mechanism, not just a quality-of-first-draft one: a spec authored by one role in isolation after the code exists tends to restate the implementation (sdd-44) rather than business intent, and a spec that restates the code can never usefully diverge from it — so it stops being able to catch drift even while technically staying 'in sync.'
rules.reviewer_criterion: Was this scenario set formulated collaboratively before or alongside the implementation, rather than derived from the finished code by a single author afterward?

rules.text: A Then step that queries the database instead of asserting an observable output is an explicit anti-pattern: 'resist that temptation.' It binds the spec to an implementation detail (the schema) rather than behaviour, so a pure storage-layer refactor with no behaviour change breaks specs that were never describing behaviour. [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference — 'Then'.] (Mechanism: sdd-20.)

predicate.spec: no Then step directly queries internal storage (database rows, internal object state) as its assertion target; it asserts on an output observable to the user or an external system.

rules.text: A When step written as a UI script ('click the blue button') rather than a domain action ('Withdraw money') fails the 'imagine it's 1922' test and smuggles implementation assumptions into the plain-English layer. The reference's fix for a step joining two actions with 'and': split into two When/And steps, one action each. [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference — 'When'; cucumber.io/docs/bdd/who-does-what/ — 'Scenarios' splitting example.] (Mechanism: sdd-19.)

predicate.spec: no When step names UI mechanics (clicks, field names, page elements) or joins two actions with 'and'; each names one domain-level action.

rules.text: Two steps whose wording collides once the leading keyword is stripped (sdd-21) — most often a Given/Then pair describing 'the same fact' in different tenses — are a vague-domain-language anti-pattern, not a tooling problem; the fix is more precise, business-specific phrasing, never a workaround bolted onto the automation layer. [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference — 'Steps'.]

predicate.spec: a step-text collision across Given/When/Then is resolved by rewording toward more specific domain language, not by adding hidden disambiguation in the step-definition layer.

rules.text: A scenario padded well past the recommended 3-5 steps (sdd-12) has usually stopped being one example of one rule and started narrating a procedure — split it, or extract genuinely incidental setup into Background (sdd-13). A scenario is only useful as living documentation if a reader can hold the whole thing in mind at once.
rules.reviewer_criterion: Does this scenario stay close to 3-5 steps and illustrate one rule — and if not, has it been reviewed for a split or a Background extraction rather than left to grow?

rules.text: Using Background to set up complicated state the reader actually needs is a misuse of the keyword — guidance is explicit: 'don't use Background to set up complicated states, unless that state is actually something the client needs to know,' preferring a higher-level step instead. A Background that has 'scrolled off the screen' defeats its own overview purpose. [VERIFIED, cucumber.io/docs/gherkin/reference — 'Tips for using Background'.] (Rule: sdd-13.)

predicate.spec: Background sections stay short enough to remain visible alongside the scenarios they support, and do not hide state the reader needs to evaluate correctness behind an opaque higher-level step where that state actually matters to the reader.

rules.text: Example Mapping's discipline (sdd-31) is the countermeasure to gold-plating: any scenario that cannot be traced back to a blue rule card that itself traces back to the yellow story card the group discussed does not belong in the spec yet. Anything that can't answer 'which rule, from which story, does this illustrate?' is speculative scope — capture it as a question instead of formulating it prematurely.
rules.reviewer_criterion: Can every scenario in this change be traced to a discussed rule and story, or does at least one exist only because it seemed like a reasonable thing to also support?

rules.text: A spec whose steps are really the implementation reworded (e.g. "the save() method returns true") fails both the ubiquitous-language test (sdd-29) and the 'imagine it's 1922' test (sdd-19, sdd-39) at once. Operational check: if a domain expert with no engineering background cannot read the scenario and confirm it's right, it is a disguised implementation note wearing Given/When/Then formatting, not a specification.
rules.reviewer_criterion: Strip the scenario of Gherkin formatting — does the remaining prose read as a business rule a domain expert could confirm, or as a description of a function/class/method?

rules.text: BDD predates and outlives Cucumber. Dan North built the first implementation, JBehave, to give the Given/When/Then acceptance-criteria template an executable 'story runner'; the same discipline produced RSpec (Ruby, via Dave Astels) and North's planned rbehave. The concrete Gherkin keyword syntax (§3) is one thoroughly-documented instance of the discovery→formulation→automation pipeline (§2) — the pipeline and acceptance-criteria discipline (§5) transfer to SpecFlow/Behave/JBehave/a team's own convention; the exact keyword grammar does not have to. [VERIFIED, dannorth.net/blog/introducing-bdd/ — 'The present and future of BDD'.]
